choices: The accessibility tree is identical to the DOM tree; there's no real difference

A second structure the browser derives from the markup, read by screen readers and other assistive tech — semantic elements populate it with a correct role/name/state automatically, while a <div> populates it as generic, with no meaningful role
The accessibility tree only exists if a screen reader is actively installed on the machine
A <div> gets the same role as a <button> automatically, since both are HTML elements
items.explanation: The accessibility tree is a parallel structure specifically for non-visual/non-mouse interaction. Semantic elements carry inherent role/name/state information into it; a <div> has no inherent role, so its entry is essentially empty regardless of how it looks visually.
items.reference:
role: generic, no info

Why: the accessibility tree only carries meaning that the tag itself declares.
items.learnMore:
The accessibility tree

Every page has two trees built from the same markup: the DOM tree, which JS and CSS operate on, and the accessibility tree, which is what screen readers, switch devices, and voice control actually read.

Semantic elements come with a built-in role, an accessible name, and state (pressed, expanded, disabled) that populate the accessibility tree automatically. A <div> has none of that built in — its entry is just "generic," no matter how it's styled to look.

Common mistake

Assuming that if a page looks right, it works right for a screen reader — visual correctness and accessibility-tree correctness are two separate things derived from the same markup.

items.learnMore:
What styling alone doesn't fix

CSS can make a

look exactly like a button — same colors, same padding, same hover state. None of that touches the two things that actually make a button usable without a mouse: being reachable via Tab, and responding to Enter or Space once focused.

Reproducing both by hand means adding tabindex="0" and a keydown handler that checks for both keys — work a real <button> needs zero lines of extra code for.

Testing only with a mouse and concluding the div 'works fine' — the failure is invisible until someone tries to use Tab and Enter instead.

items.prompt: Implement `isKeyboardAccessible(el)` from L3: `el` is `{ tag, href?, tabIndex?, hasKeyHandler? }`. Native interactive tags (button, input, select, textarea) are always accessible; an `a` tag is only accessible if it has a non-empty `href`; any other tag is only accessible if it has BOTH `tabIndex === 0` AND `hasKeyHandler === true`.

tests.description: a link with an href is accessible
a link with no href is NOT accessible
a bare div with an onclick-style handler is not accessible
a div with only tabIndex (no key handler) is still not accessible
a div with both tabIndex and a key handler is accessible

items.explanation: This encodes the real rule browsers apply: most native interactive elements are unconditionally accessible, `a` depends on actually being a link (a real href), and anything else only counts if BOTH the focus stop and the key handling were added by hand — missing either one leaves it broken for keyboard users, which is exactly the gap that makes native elements simpler than reimplementing them.
items.reference:
isKeyboardAccessible rule
TagCondition
button/input/select/textareaalways true
atrue only if href is non-empty
anything elsetabIndex === 0 AND hasKeyHandler === true

Why: the rule is checkable as plain data, independent of any real DOM.
items.learnMore:
Modeling keyboard accessibility as data

The rule reduces to: is this a native interactive element (always accessible, with needing a real href), or does it have BOTH an explicit tabindex AND matching keydown handling manually added?

Modeling it this way — as plain objects, not a live DOM — is exactly what lets it be unit tested without a browser at all.

Common mistake

Checking only tabIndex === 0 without also checking hasKeyHandler (or vice versa) — either one alone leaves the element broken; both must be true together for a non-native tag.

items.prompt: Implement `semanticTagFor(role)` mapping a logical content role to its correct HTML tag: 'primary-action' -> 'button', 'internal-link' -> 'a', 'external-link' -> 'a', 'page-heading' -> 'h1', 'top-navigation' -> 'nav', 'main-content' -> 'main'. For any unrecognized role, return 'div'.

tests.description: unrecognized role falls back to div

items.explanation: A lookup table is the honest model of what refactoring div-soup actually is: every div already has an intended role in the author's head, and fixing the markup is just making that mapping explicit and consistent instead of ad hoc. The div fallback matches L1/L2's rule that div is correct only when no role fits.
items.reference:
Role → tag mapping
Logical roleCorrect tag
primary-actionbutton
internal-link / external-linka
page-headingh1
top-navigationnav
main-contentmain

Why: each logical role maps to exactly one correct tag — this is the refactor from div-soup to semantic HTML, expressed as a pure function.
items.learnMore:
Refactoring is a lookup, not a rewrite

Converting a div-soup page to semantic HTML is, at its core, a mapping problem: every element already has an intended role (it's the primary button, it's a nav link, it's the page heading) — the refactor is replacing

with whatever tag matches that role.

Modeling this as a pure function makes the refactor mechanical and testable, rather than something re-derived from scratch by eye on every page.

a page-heading rendered as h1 is correct, not misused
a decorative-wrapper role rendered as div is fine (div IS the correct tag)

items.prompt: Implement `hasSkippedHeadingLevel(levels)`: `levels` is an array of heading numbers in document order (e.g. [1,2,3]). Return true if any consecutive pair jumps by more than one level (e.g. h2 directly to h4).

tests.description: h1 to h2 to h4 skips h3
h1 straight to h3 skips h2
going back up a level is not a skip

items.explanation: Only forward jumps (increasing level) can skip — going back up to a shallower level (e.g. h3 back to h2) is always valid, since it's just closing a subsection, not opening a new one out of order. The check only has to compare each consecutive pair once.
items.reference:
Heading level skip
SequenceSkip?
h1, h2, h3no
h1, h2, h4yes — skips h3
h1, h3yes — skips h2

Why: a skip is any jump of more than one level between consecutive headings, checked in document order.
items.learnMore:
Why heading hierarchy is checkable structure, not styling

Screen readers offer a "jump by heading level" navigation mode, and some assistive tech explicitly flags skipped levels as a structural error, because sighted users get an implicit outline from font-size cues that a skipped level breaks for anyone navigating by heading semantics alone.

The check is purely structural: given a sequence of heading levels in document order, does any consecutive pair jump by more than one level? No visual rendering is needed to answer that.

Common mistake

Assuming heading levels are just about font size — choosing h3 because 'it looks the right size' instead of because it's genuinely one level below the nearest h2 creates exactly this kind of skip.

items.prompt: Implement `firstSkippedHeadingIndex(levels)`: same skip rule as hasSkippedHeadingLevel, but return the index of the first heading that causes a skip (i.e. the index of levels[i] where the jump from levels[i-1] happens), or -1 if there's no skip.

tests.description: finds the FIRST skip, not a later one

items.explanation: Same forward-jump rule as hasSkippedHeadingLevel, but returning the position instead of a boolean — this is the shape a real linter needs to actually point a developer at the specific offending heading rather than just saying 'something's wrong somewhere'.

items.prompt: Implement `countLandmarks(tags)`: `tags` is an array of tag name strings. Return how many of them are recognized landmark elements: header, nav, main, footer, aside.
items.explanation: A fixed Set lookup is the correct model here — landmark status isn't fuzzy or stylable, it's a closed list of five tag names, so membership testing against that exact set is both correct and the simplest possible implementation.
items.reference:
🧭 header/nav/main/footer/aside — recognized landmarks
📦 div/span — never landmarks, regardless of class name

Why: landmark status is a fixed set of tag names — nothing else counts, no matter how it's styled.
items.learnMore:
Counting landmarks as a structural check

Landmark status depends only on the tag name, from a fixed set: header, nav, main, footer, aside. A div styled or classed to look like a landmark region doesn't count, because the assistive-tech shortcut reads tags, not classes.

This makes 'does this page have real landmarks' a checkable, tag-based question — exactly the shape of check an automated linter runs before a human ever tests with a screen reader.

items.prompt: Implement `hasMainLandmark(tags)`: `tags` is an array of tag name strings. Return true if exactly one 'main' tag is present, false if it's missing or if there's more than one (a page should have exactly one <main>).
items.explanation: A page is supposed to have exactly one <main> — zero means there's no landmark for 'jump to main content' to land on, and more than one makes that same jump ambiguous, so both edges are treated as failing, not just the missing case.

items.prompt: Implement `isFullyAccessibleInteractiveDiv(el)`: `el` is `{ tag, role?, tabIndex?, hasKeyHandler? }`. Per L3's failure modes, a div/span standing in for a button is only fully accessible if it has role === 'button' AND tabIndex === 0 AND hasKeyHandler === true — all three, not any subset. For any non-div/span tag, return true (native elements don't need this check).

tests.description: a div with only role set is not fully accessible
a div with role and tabIndex but no key handler is not fully accessible
a div with all three pieces is fully accessible
tests.expr: expect(isFullyAccessibleInteractiveDiv({ tag: 'div', role: 'button', tabIndex: 0, hasKeyHandler: true })).toBe(true)

items.explanation: This is L3's third failure mode as code: role='button' alone only fixes the announced role, and tabIndex alone only fixes focus — none of the three pieces (role, focus, key handling) is individually sufficient, all three have to hold together, exactly like the native button they're trying to replicate.
